messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Psychologist
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 61

He is a 37-year-old African man who works as a psychologist, and when he first begins talking about what happened, he does so with the careful precision he uses with his own clients. He speaks in a steady voice, but there is a tightness in his jaw and a habit of looking toward the door that suggests how much effort it takes to stay present. The assault happened several months ago, after an evening that began in a familiar, ordinary way. He had gone out briefly, expecting to return home, and instead found himself in a situation that turned dangerous quickly. What followed was rape, an experience that shattered his sense of control and left him with a profound feeling of having been trapped inside his own body while someone else decided what happened to it.

In the immediate aftermath, he moves through the world in a kind of stunned disbelief. He does not tell many people. He isolates himself, cancels social plans, and begins to live in a narrower and narrower orbit. As a single man, he is used to privacy and self-reliance, but now that independence feels less like strength and more like a wall he cannot get through. He tries to return to work because he believes he should be able to function, especially given his profession, yet being a psychologist becomes unexpectedly painful. When clients speak about fear, violation, or loss of control, he feels a sudden internal pressure, as if the room is closing in. He maintains his role, offers reflection, asks questions, and appears composed, but afterward he is often exhausted in a way that has little to do with the session itself. He sits in his car before going home, unable to move, or he walks through his apartment and feels detached from everything around him, as if he is moving through a life that no longer fully belongs to him.

Sleep becomes unreliable. He lies awake replaying the night in fragments, not always in order, not always with the same details, but with the same sickening sense that it is happening again. When he does sleep, he wakes abruptly from dreams that leave him sweating and disoriented, his heart racing before he is fully conscious. He becomes hyperaware of sound and movement: footsteps in a hallway, a voice too close behind him, the slam of a door. He startles more easily than he used to and finds himself scanning spaces automatically, mapping exits, checking who is near him. This vigilance follows him everywhere. Even in safe settings, his body acts as though danger is imminent.

He also notices changes in how he relates to himself. There are moments when he feels shame so dense that it seems to sit physically in his chest. He struggles with thoughts about why he was there, what he should have done differently, and how he could not prevent what happened. These thoughts are harsh and repetitive, and he knows, intellectually, how he would challenge them in a client, but knowing does not stop them from arriving. He feels anger too, though it is often buried under numbness. At times, the numbness becomes so complete that he feels unable to access pleasure, grief, or even clear emotion. He describes himself as functioning on autopilot, going through routines without real engagement. Meals are skipped. Exercise becomes sporadic. He avoids places that remind him of the assault and finds himself taking longer routes home or declining invitations that would require him to be alone with unfamiliar people.

In sessions, he is able to connect the assault to earlier beliefs about competence, masculinity, and safety, though he does so cautiously. He speaks about the disorienting experience of surviving a violation that conflicts so deeply with how he understands himself. As a professional who spends his life helping others make sense of trauma, he is unsettled by how little comfort his own expertise provides. At times he feels embarrassed by that, as though he should be able to manage better because he knows the language of trauma. But the language does not protect him from the body memories, the dread, the nightmares, or the persistent sense that the world has become less predictable and less safe.

Over time, he begins to describe small signs that his life is not entirely frozen. He comes to sessions more regularly. He speaks a little more freely about his fear and grief. He notices moments when he is able to stay in a room without checking the exits repeatedly, or when he finishes a day of work without needing to disappear immediately afterward. Even so, the trauma remains close to the surface, shaping how he sleeps, how he moves, and how he sees himself. He is still living with the aftermath of a night that divided his life into before and after, and each day requires him to negotiate that divide in quiet, exhausting ways.
